recent_posts.title: DeskPi Super4C review and SBC cluster value reality check
recent_posts.summary: Jeff Geerling reviews the DeskPi Super4C, a 4-node Raspberry Pi CM5 cluster board that improves on the older Super6C with remote management via ESP32 and redundant Ethernet/power inputs. He benchmarks it against student clusters from the SBCC 2026 competition, where university teams competed with $6,000 HPC cluster budgets. The Super4C lands in the middle of the pack for both HPL performance and efficiency. Geerling is candid that SBC clusters offer poor value compared to mini PCs — a minimum build costs ~$600 and his full setup ran ~$1,400 — but argues they're worthwhile for learning HPC, edge computing experiments, or ARM build farms at desk scale.

recent_posts.title: Raspberry Pi Connect may control Windows soon
recent_posts.summary: Raspberry Pi Connect, the free remote access service from Raspberry Pi, may soon support Windows PCs. An unofficial Windows daemon is available for testing via the Raspberry Pi forums, built on Go and using WebRTC and VNC standards. Current issues include mouse cursor offset, occasional freezing, Task Manager conflicts, and resolution quirks. Remote Shell access works and supports Command Prompt, PowerShell, and WSL. macOS support may also be coming. Pi Connect's Organizations plan at $0.50/device/month could undercut competitors like RealVNC for small fleets.

recent_posts.title: RTL8159-based 10G USB adapters reviewed as Thunderbolt alternatives
recent_posts.summary: RTL8159-based 10G USB 3.2 adapters are now available for around $80, offering a smaller, cooler, and cheaper alternative to bulky Thunderbolt 10GbE adapters. Testing across four machines (Framework 13, MacBook Neo, M4 MacBook Air, AMD desktop) shows full 10 Gbps is only achievable with a USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 (20 Gbps) port; other machines top out at 6-7 Gbps. Mac support is plug-and-play, while Windows requires a manual Realtek driver install. Thermals are notably better than Aquantia-based adapters, peaking at 42.5°C. For most users without a 20 Gbps USB port, a 2.5G or 5G adapter remains better value, but for those with a 10G network and compatible port, this is a compelling compact option.

recent_posts.title: An Arm Mainboard for the Framework Laptop
recent_posts.summary: Jeff Geerling reviews the MetaComputing AI PC Mainboard, an Arm-based mainboard for the Framework 13 laptop featuring Cix's P1 CP8180 SoC with 12 cores and up to 32 GB of soldered LPDDR5 RAM. The board runs Ubuntu 25.04 with full hardware support, including the Mali G720 Immortalis iGPU for Vulkan/OpenGL. Benchmarks show competitive multi-core performance but weaker single-core scores compared to Apple Silicon, and it falls short of Framework's own Ryzen AI 5 340 mainboard in both single and multi-core performance. Gaming via FEX x86 emulation on Steam is possible but choppy and largely unplayable. At $550 (pushed higher by the DRAM crisis), the board is recommended only for Arm enthusiasts and developers, not general users seeking value.

recent_posts.title: Build your own Dial-up ISP with a Raspberry Pi
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on project guide for building a local dial-up ISP using a Raspberry Pi, a USB 56K modem, and a telephone line simulator. The setup uses mgetty and PPP on Debian Linux to handle modem calls and authenticate connections. An Ansible playbook automates the configuration. The project goes further by connecting a vintage 1999 Apple iBook G3 wirelessly via an original AirPort Base Station, achieving 33.6 kbps dial-up over 802.11b Wi-Fi. Macproxy Classic is used to make modern websites accessible on old browsers. The author reflects on how the project deepened understanding of modem protocols, QAM, and modern networking concepts like VPNs.

recent_posts.title: DRAM pricing is killing the hobbyist SBC market
recent_posts.summary: Raspberry Pi has announced new price increases driven by LPDDR4 DRAM costs, pushing the 16GB Pi 5 to $299.99 and a 3GB Pi 4 to $83.75. LPDDR chips now account for the majority of board cost across SBC vendors. The author argues the hobbyist SBC market is dying as high-RAM boards become unaffordable, new board launches have slowed (only Radxa showed some cadence recently), and even mini PCs have crossed $250 for 8GB models. The author is shifting toward older SBCs and microcontrollers, and worries smaller vendors won't survive the prolonged pricing pressure even if Raspberry Pi can weather it through its microcontroller and industrial business.

recent_posts.title: Bring back MiniDV with this Raspberry Pi FireWire HAT
recent_posts.summary: A guide to building a portable MiniDV Memory Recording Unit (MRU) using a Raspberry Pi 5, a FireWire HAT (Firehat), and a PiSugar3 Plus battery. The setup replaces expensive legacy Sony MRUs (~$300 on eBay) with a ~$150-200 DIY alternative. It requires recompiling the Linux kernel to enable FireWire support, then installing the Firehat software. The device can record directly from FireWire/i.Link cameras, archive MiniDV tapes via dvgrab, and transfer files over WiFi or USB. Two FireWire controllers are confirmed working on Pi 5: TI XIO2213A and VIA VT6315N. Linux kernel FireWire support is guaranteed until at least 2029.

recent_posts.title: Using FireWire on a Raspberry Pi
recent_posts.summary: Apple's removal of FireWire (IEEE 1394) support in macOS 26 Tahoe prompted exploration of a Linux-based alternative using a Raspberry Pi 5. By adding a Mini PCIe HAT and a StarTech FireWire adapter, the Pi can recognize FireWire controllers. However, using them requires recompiling the Linux kernel with CONFIG_FIREWIRE and CONFIG_FIREWIRE_OHCI enabled, and configuring the Pi's PCIe bus for 32-bit DMA support (since old FireWire controllers lack 64-bit access). Once set up, the dvgrab tool can capture DV footage from cameras like the Canon GL1, and can be scripted for automation projects.

recent_posts.title: Ranking the best Apple laptop ever made across Mac history
recent_posts.summary: Jeff Geerling argues the 11" MacBook Air is the best laptop Apple ever made, citing its ahead-of-its-time design and surprising repairability. He also gathered opinions from other Mac YouTubers, whose picks range from the iBook G3 Clamshell and Titanium PowerBook G4 to the modern M-series MacBooks. The post touches on repairability across Mac eras, noting that older machines were more upgradeable while modern Apple Silicon laptops prioritize thinness and efficiency over serviceability.

recent_posts.title: Restoring an Xserve G5: When Apple built real servers
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on restoration of an Apple Xserve G5 (RackMac3,1) from 2004, covering PSU recapping to fix capacitor plague, SATA drive compatibility quirks, power consumption (~140W idle), noise levels, and installing Mac OS X Server 10.3. The post also explores the machine's unique hardware features like its worm-gear drive lock and DB9 serial console port, with a future goal of using it as a GPS-based precision time server.
